title: Hebrews

stories.title: 📜 Hebrews 1
summaryBullets: On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. (1:1).
But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe. (1:2).

The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word. After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. (1:3).
So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs. (1:4).
For to which of the angels did God ever say: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father”? Or again: “I will be His Father, and He will be My Son”? (1:5).
And again, when God brings His firstborn into the world, He says: “Let all God’s angels worship Him.” (1:6).
Now about the angels He says: “He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire.” (1:7).
But about the Son He says: “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom. (1:8).
You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, Your God, has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy.” (1:9).
And: “In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. (1:10).
They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment. (1:11).
You will roll them up like a robe; like a garment they will be changed; but You remain the same, and Your years will never end.” (1:12).
Yet to which of the angels did God ever say: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet”? (1:13).
Are not the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation? (1:14).
crossRefs: Psalm 2:7: The LORD tells His anointed king, You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.
2 Samuel 7:14: God promises David of his offspring, I will be his Father, and he will be My son.
Psalm 45:6-7: A royal psalm addresses the king, Your throne, O God, endures forever, and speaks of the oil of joy.
Psalm 102:25-27: The LORD laid the foundations of the earth; the heavens wear out like a garment, but He remains the same.
Psalm 110:1: The LORD says to David's Lord, Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זִיו הַכָּבוֹד (zîw hakkāḇōd, sense), Greek: ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης (apaugasma tēs dóxēs, NT), Aramaic: זיוא דיקרא (zīwā diyqarā)
translationNotes.note: Phrase describes the Son as the shining forth or exact expression of God’s divine glory.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל (kōhēn gādōl), Greek: ἀρχιερεύς (archiereús, NT), Aramaic: כהנא רבא (kahnā rabbā)
translationNotes.note: Title for chief priest of Israel; here applied to Jesus as mediator between God and humans.

In a royal court the place at the king's right hand belonged to the second in command, the officer who acted with the king's authority. When Solomon's mother came to him he had a throne brought and set at his right hand (1 Kings 2:19). Hebrews 1:13 quotes Psalm 110:1, where the LORD tells David's Lord to sit at His right hand, and the letter returns to that seat four more times (1:3, 8:1, 10:12, 12:2).

The picture behind a footstool for your feet is a beaten enemy under the victor's foot. Joshua made his commanders put their feet on the necks of five captured kings (Joshua 10:24), and Egyptian royal furniture was built to say the same thing: a footstool from Tutankhamun's tomb is carved with bound foreign captives where the king's feet rested. Hebrews quotes the line from Psalm 110:1 twice, at 1:13 and 10:13.

stories.keyTakeaway: God has now spoken through his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things and through whom he made the universe; the Son is the radiance of God's glory and is superior to the angels. Scripture shows the Son sitting at God's right hand, with the angels as ministering spirits serving those who inherit salvation.

stories.title: 📜 Hebrews 2
summaryBullets: We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. (2:1).
For if the message spoken by angels was binding, and every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment, (2:2).
how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? This salvation was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him, (2:3).
and was affirmed by God through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will. (2:4).
For it is not to angels that He has subjected the world to come, about which we are speaking. (2:5).
But somewhere it is testified in these words: “What is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him? (2:6).
You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor (2:7).
and placed everything under his feet.” When God subjected all things to him, He left nothing outside of his control. Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him. (2:8).
But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone. (2:9).
In bringing many sons to glory, it was fitting for God, for whom and through whom all things exist, to make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering. (2:10).
For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers. (2:11).
He says: “I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly.” (2:12).
And again: “I will put My trust in Him.” And once again: “Here am I, and the children God has given Me.” (2:13).
Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, (2:14).
and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death. (2:15).
For surely it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham. (2:16).

For this reason He had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God, in order to make atonement for the sins of the people. (2:17).
Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted. (2:18).
crossRefs: Psalm 8:4-6: What is man that You are mindful of him? You made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and put everything under his feet.
Psalm 22:22: The sufferer vows to proclaim God's name to his brothers and praise Him in the assembly.
Isaiah 8:17-18: Isaiah waits for the LORD and says, Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me.
Galatians 3:19: Paul says the law was administered through angels by a mediator until the promised Seed came.
Genesis 3:15: God tells the serpent that the woman's offspring will crush his head.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זִיו הַכָּבוֹד (zîw hakkāḇōd, sense), Greek: ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης (apaugasma tēs dóxēs, NT), Aramaic: זיוא דיקרא (zīwā diyqarā)
translationNotes.note: Phrase describes the Son as the shining forth or exact expression of God’s divine glory.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל (kōhēn gādōl), Greek: ἀρχιερεύς (archiereús, NT), Aramaic: כהנא רבא (kahnā rabbā)
translationNotes.note: Title for chief priest of Israel; here applied to Jesus as mediator between God and humans.

translationNotes.term: A little lower than the angels
translationNotes.original: Greek: βραχύ τι (brachy ti) - Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים (elohim)
translationNotes.note: Hebrews 2:6-8 quotes Psalm 8:4-6 from the Greek Old Testament, which reads lower than the angels where the Hebrew of Psalm 8:5 reads lower than elohim. The Greek phrase brachy ti can mean a little in rank or a little while in time, and 2:9 uses it both ways: Jesus was made lower, and is now crowned with glory and honour because He suffered death.

The word translated angel means messenger. The message in 2:2 is the law given at Sinai, which the New Testament says repeatedly was delivered through angels: Stephen charges Israel with receiving the law ordained by angels (Acts 7:53), and Paul says it was administered through angels by a mediator (Galatians 3:19). Deuteronomy 33:2 describes the LORD coming from Sinai with ten thousands of holy ones.

stories.keyTakeaway: Believers must heed the salvation announced by Jesus and confirmed through miracles and the Holy Spirit, lest they drift away; Jesus was made lower than angels and suffered death to perfect salvation and free humanity from fear of death, becoming a merciful high priest who helps those being tempted.

stories.title: 🌿 Hebrews 3
summaryBullets: Therefore, holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling, set your focus on Jesus, the apostle and high priest whom we confess. (3:1).
He was faithful to the One who appointed Him, just as Moses was faithful in all God’s house. (3:2).
For Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself. (3:3).
And every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything. (3:4).
Now Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house, testifying to what would be spoken later. (3:5).
But Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house. And we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast. (3:6).
Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear His voice, (3:7).
do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion, in the day of testing in the wilderness, (3:8).
where your fathers tested and tried Me, and for forty years saw My works. (3:9).
Therefore I was angry with that generation, and I said, ‘Their hearts are always going astray, and they have not known My ways.’ (3:10).
So I swore on oath in My anger, ‘They shall never enter My rest.’” (3:11).
See to it, brothers, that none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God. (3:12).
But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness. (3:13).
We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first. (3:14).
As it has been said: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion.” (3:15).
For who were the ones who heard and rebelled? Were they not all those Moses led out of Egypt? (3:16).
And with whom was God angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? (3:17).
And to whom did He swear that they would never enter His rest? Was it not to those who disobeyed? (3:18).
So we see that it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter. (3:19).
crossRefs: Numbers 12:7: God defends Moses, saying he is faithful in all My house and that He speaks with him face to face.
Psalm 95:7-11: Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts as at Meribah, in the day of testing in the wilderness.
Exodus 17:1-7: Israel quarrels with Moses for water at Rephidim, and the place is named Massah and Meribah.
Numbers 14:20-35: The LORD swears that the generation that refused to enter Canaan will fall in the wilderness over forty years.
2 Samuel 7:11-16: David offers to build the LORD a house, and God answers that He will build David a house instead.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְנוּחָה (mĕnūḥāh), Greek: κατάπαυσις (katápausis, NT), Aramaic: ניחא (nīḥā)
translationNotes.note: Word used for rest, settlement, or Sabbath; in Hebrews, refers to God’s promised spiritual rest.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְרִיבָה (Meribah), מַסָּה (Massah) - Greek: παραπικρασμός (parapikrasmos), πειρασμός (peirasmos)
translationNotes.note: Psalm 95:8, quoted here, names two places. Meribah means quarrelling and Massah means testing, and both names were given at Rephidim, where Israel had no water and turned on Moses (Exodus 17:1-7); a second quarrel at Kadesh got the name Meribah again (Numbers 20:1-13). The Greek Old Testament translated the two place names rather than keeping them, which is why Hebrews 3:8 reads the rebellion and the day of testing instead of Meribah and Massah.

The forty years were a sentence, not a slow journey. Twelve men scouted Canaan for forty days, and when the people refused to go in, the LORD gave them one year in the wilderness for each day (Numbers 14:33-34). Every man counted in the census from twenty years old and up died there except Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:29-30, 26:64-65), which is what 3:17 means by bodies falling in the wilderness.

The Hebrew and Greek words for house mean the building, the household living in it, and the family line, all at once. Numbers 12:7, quoted at 3:2, says Moses was faithful in all God's house. The same double sense drives 2 Samuel 7:5-16, where David offers to build the LORD a house of cedar and is told that the LORD will build David a house instead.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jesus deserves greater honor than Moses because he is God's Son over his house, not merely a faithful servant within it; the author warns believers not to harden their hearts like the Israelites who rebelled in the wilderness and were denied God's rest.

headings.text: Jesus Our Apostle and High Priest

stories.title: 🌿 Hebrews 4
summaryBullets: Therefore, while the promise of entering His rest still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it. (4:1).
For we also received the good news just as they did; but the message they heard was of no value to them, since they did not share the faith of those who comprehended it. (4:2).

Now we who have believed enter that rest. As for the others, it is just as God has said: “So I swore on oath in My anger, ‘They shall never enter My rest.’” And yet His works have been finished since the foundation of the world. (4:3).
For somewhere He has spoken about the seventh day in this manner: “And on the seventh day God rested from all His works.” (4:4).
And again, as He says in the passage above: “They shall never enter My rest.” (4:5).
Since, then, it remains for some to enter His rest, and since those who formerly heard the good news did not enter because of their disobedience, (4:6).
God again designated a certain day as “Today,” when a long time later He spoke through David as was just stated: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.” (4:7).
For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day. (4:8).
There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God. (4:9).
For whoever enters God’s rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His. (4:10).
Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one will fall by following the same pattern of disobedience. (4:11).

For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart. (4:12).
Nothing in all creation is hidden from God’s sight; everything is uncovered and exposed before the eyes of Him to whom we must give account. (4:13).
Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to what we profess. (4:14).
For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin. (4:15).
Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need. (4:16).
crossRefs: Genesis 2:2-3: On the seventh day God finished His work and rested, and He blessed the seventh day and set it apart.
Joshua 21:43-45: The LORD gave Israel the whole land and rest on every side, and not one of His good promises failed.
Isaiah 49:2: The LORD made the servant's mouth like a sharpened sword and hid him in the shadow of His hand.
Exodus 25:22: God tells Moses He will meet him above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim, and speak with him there.
Isaiah 53:9: The servant had done no violence, and no deceit was found in his mouth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְנוּחָה (mĕnūḥāh), Greek: κατάπαυσις (katápausis, NT), Aramaic: ניחא (nīḥā)
translationNotes.note: Word used for rest, settlement, or Sabbath; in Hebrews, refers to God’s promised spiritual rest.

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

The word in 4:9 is not the word for rest used everywhere else in the chapter. It is built on the verb to keep sabbath and it appears nowhere else in the Greek Bible. The Greek Old Testament uses that verb for the land itself keeping its sabbaths while Israel was in exile (Leviticus 26:34-35, 2 Chronicles 36:21), so the word carries observance, not just the absence of work.

Joshua and Jesus are the same name. Hebrew Yehoshua, meaning the LORD saves, comes into Greek as Iesous, so 4:8 has the identical word this letter uses for Jesus everywhere else and a translator has to decide which man is meant. The argument settles it: Joshua son of Nun did bring Israel into the land (Joshua 21:43-45), yet centuries later David still spoke of a rest to be entered today.

stories.keyTakeaway: God's rest remains available to believers who have faith and obey, unlike those in the past who fell short through disobedience; the word of God penetrates all things and judges hearts, and Jesus as high priest empathizes with human weakness without having sinned.

stories.title: 🕊️ Hebrews 5
summaryBullets: Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. (5:1).
He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is subject to weakness. (5:2).
That is why he is obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins, as well as for the sins of the people. (5:3).
No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was. (5:4).
So also Christ did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest, but He was called by the One who said to Him: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.” (5:5).
And in another passage God says: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” (5:6).
During the days of Jesus’ earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence. (5:7).
Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered. (5:8).
And having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him (5:9).
and was designated by God as high priest in the order of Melchizedek. (5:10).
We have much to say about this, but it is hard to explain, because you are dull of hearing. (5:11).
Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to reteach you the basic principles of God’s word. You need milk, not solid food! (5:12).
For everyone who lives on milk is still an infant, inexperienced in the message of righteousness. (5:13).
But solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil. (5:14).
crossRefs: Exodus 28:1: Aaron and his sons are set apart from among the Israelites to serve God as priests.
Leviticus 16:6: On the Day of Atonement the high priest first offers a bull as a sin offering for himself and his household.
Numbers 16:1-40: Korah and his company seize priestly office they were not given, and the ground swallows them.
Psalm 110:4: The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind, You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.
Luke 22:41-44: In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the cup be taken from Him, and prays more earnestly in anguish.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק (Malkî-ṣedeq), Greek: Μελχισεδέκ (Melchisedék, NT), Aramaic: מלכי צדקא (Malkī ṣidqā)
translationNotes.note: Name means 'king of righteousness'; king of Salem, priest of God Most High, type for Christ’s eternal priesthood.

translationNotes.term: Called by God, as Aaron was
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִלֻּאִים (millu'im) - Hebrew: מִלֵּא יָד (mille yad)
translationNotes.note: Priests were installed by a seven-day ceremony (Exodus 29, Leviticus 8) in which blood was put on the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe of each man and oil was poured over his head. The Hebrew idiom for ordaining is to fill the hand, and the ram used is called the ram of filling. Taking the office uninvited was fatal: Korah and his company were destroyed for it (Numbers 16:1-40) and King Uzziah was struck with leprosy for burning incense in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16-21).

The verb in 5:14 is the one behind the English word gymnasium; it is what an athlete does in training, not what a student does at a desk. It runs with the milk and solid food image of 5:12-13: an infant is fed, an adult chews. The letter comes back to athletic language at 12:1, where the Christian life is a race run in a stadium.

translationNotes.term: Learned obedience from what He suffered
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἔμαθεν ἀφ' ὧν ἔπαθεν (emathen aph' hon epathen)
translationNotes.note: The two Greek verbs differ by one letter: emathen, he learned, and epathen, he suffered. It is a fixed pairing in Greek and the English cannot carry it; Aeschylus uses the same play in the Agamemnon, pathei mathos, learning by suffering. Hebrews 2:10 states the matching idea, the author of their salvation made perfect through sufferings.

stories.keyTakeaway: A high priest is chosen from among people to represent them before God; Christ did not claim this honor himself but was appointed by God and designated priest in the order of Melchizedek through his prayers, suffering, and obedience. The author notes his readers have become dull and need basic instruction again rather than the deeper teaching they should be ready to receive.

stories.title: 🕊️ Hebrews 6
summaryBullets: Therefore let us leave the elementary teachings about Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith in God, (6:1).
instruction about baptisms, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. (6:2).
And this we will do, if God permits. (6:3).
It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit, (6:4).
who have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age — (6:5).
and then have fallen away — to be restored to repentance, because they themselves are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame. (6:6).
For land that drinks in the rain often falling on it and that produces a crop useful to those for whom it is tended receives the blessing of God. (6:7).
But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless, and its curse is imminent. In the end it will be burned. (6:8).
Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your case— things that accompany salvation. (6:9).
For God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name as you have ministered to the saints and continue to do so. (6:10).
We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure. (6:11).
Then you will not be sluggish, but will imitate those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised. (6:12).
When God made His promise to Abraham, since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself, (6:13).
saying, “I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants.” (6:14).
And so Abraham, after waiting patiently, obtained the promise. (6:15).
Men swear by someone greater than themselves, and their oath serves as a confirmation to end all argument. (6:16).
So when God wanted to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise, He guaranteed it with an oath. (6:17).
Thus by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged. (6:18).
We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, (6:19).
where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. (6:20).
crossRefs: Numbers 27:18-23: Moses lays his hands on Joshua before the priest and the whole assembly and commissions him.
Numbers 14:22-23: Those who saw God's glory and signs in Egypt and still tested Him ten times will not see the land.
Genesis 3:17-18: The ground is cursed because of Adam and will bring forth thorns and thistles.
Genesis 22:16-17: The LORD swears by Himself, since there is no one greater, to bless Abraham and multiply his offspring.
Leviticus 16:2: The LORD warns Aaron not to enter behind the veil whenever he chooses, or he will die.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק (Malkî-ṣedeq), Greek: Μελχισεδέκ (Melchisedék, NT), Aramaic: מלכי צדקא (Malkī ṣidqā)
translationNotes.note: Name means 'king of righteousness'; king of Salem, priest of God Most High, type for Christ’s eternal priesthood.

The plural word in 6:2 is the general term for ritual washings, not the usual word for Christian baptism. Washing was ordinary life under the law: after contact with a corpse, after childbirth, after skin disease, and before priestly service (Leviticus 14-15, Numbers 19). Stepped immersion pools cut into bedrock have been excavated by the southern steps of the Temple Mount and across Jerusalem, Qumran, and Galilee, so a reader in the first century pictured a flight of steps down into water, not a font.

Ancient anchors were wooden hooks weighted with lead or pierced stone, and a ship in trouble dropped several at once: the crew on Paul's ship let out four from the stern and prayed for daylight (Acts 27:29). Hebrews 6:19 then puts the anchor somewhere no anchor goes, inside the veil of the sanctuary, the room the high priest entered once a year and no one else entered at all (Leviticus 16:2).

translationNotes.original: Greek: ὤμοσεν καθ' ἑαυτοῦ (omosen kath' heautou) - Hebrew: בִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי (bi nishbati)
translationNotes.note: An oath named something greater than the swearer as its guarantee, which is the point of 6:16, that men swear by someone greater. Hebrews 6:13-14 quotes Genesis 22:16-17, spoken at the binding of Isaac: by Myself I have sworn. There was nothing greater to name.

stories.keyTakeaway: The author urges readers to move beyond basic Christian teaching toward maturity and warns that those who have tasted God's grace and then fallen away cannot be restored to repentance. God's promise to Abraham, confirmed by oath, serves as an anchor of hope; Jesus has entered the heavenly sanctuary as a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

stories.title: 🕊️ Hebrews 7
summaryBullets: This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, (7:1).
and Abraham apportioned to him a tenth of everything. First, his name means “king of righteousness.” Then also, “king of Salem” means “king of peace.” (7:2).
Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time. (7:3).
Consider how great Melchizedek was: Even the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the plunder. (7:4).
Now the law commands the sons of Levi who become priests to collect a tenth from the people — that is, from their brothers — though they too are descended from Abraham. (7:5).
But Melchizedek, who did not trace his descent from Levi, collected a tenth from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. (7:6).
And indisputably, the lesser is blessed by the greater. (7:7).
In the case of the Levites, mortal men collect the tenth; but in the case of Melchizedek, it is affirmed that he lives on. (7:8).
And so to speak, Levi, who collects the tenth, paid the tenth through Abraham. (7:9).
For when Melchizedek met Abraham, Levi was still in the loin of his ancestor. (7:10).

Now if perfection could have been attained through the Levitical priesthood ( for on this basis the people received the law), why was there still need for another priest to appear — one in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron? (7:11).
For when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed as well. (7:12).
He of whom these things are said belonged to a different tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. (7:13).
For it is clear that our Lord descended from Judah, a tribe as to which Moses said nothing about priests. (7:14).
And this point is even more clear if another priest like Melchizedek appears, (7:15).
one who has become a priest not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life. (7:16).
For it is testified: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” (7:17).
So the former commandment is set aside because it was weak and useless (7:18).
( for the law made nothing perfect), and a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God. (7:19).
And none of this happened without an oath. For others became priests without an oath, (7:20).
but Jesus became a priest with an oath by the One who said to Him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind: ‘You are a priest forever.’” (7:21).
Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant. (7:22).
Now there have been many other priests, since death prevented them from continuing in office. (7:23).
But because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood. (7:24).
Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them. (7:25).
Such a high priest truly befits us — One who is holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. (7:26).

Unlike the other high priests, He does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people; He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself. (7:27).
For the law appoints as high priests men who are weak; but the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect forever. (7:28).
crossRefs: Genesis 14:18-20: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth.
Psalm 110:4: The LORD swears an oath He will not take back, You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.
Numbers 18:21-24: The Levites are given the tithe of Israel as their inheritance, because they receive no land of their own.
Ezra 2:61-63: Priests who cannot produce their genealogical records are excluded from the priesthood as unclean.
Genesis 49:10: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק (Malkî-ṣedeq), Greek: Μελχισεδέκ (Melchisedék, NT), Aramaic: מלכי צדקא (Malkī ṣidqā)
translationNotes.note: Name means 'king of righteousness'; king of Salem, priest of God Most High, type for Christ’s eternal priesthood.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַחַת לְעוֹלָם (ʾaḥat ləʿōlām, sense), Greek: ἐφάπαξ (ephápax, NT), Aramaic: חדא לעלמין (ḥadā l-ʿālmīn)
translationNotes.note: Means 'a single act valid forever'; used for Christ’s unique, unrepeatable sacrifice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁלֵם (Shalem) - Hebrew: אֵל עֶלְיוֹן (El Elyon)
translationNotes.note: Melchizedek appears in only two Old Testament passages. Genesis 14:18-20 has him meet Abram coming back from rescuing Lot, bring out bread and wine, bless him as priest of God Most High, and receive a tenth; then he leaves the account without another word about him. Psalm 110:4 is the only other mention, and Hebrews quotes it at 5:6, 6:20, and 7:17. Salem is Jerusalem: Psalm 76:2 sets God's dwelling in Salem and in Zion.

The Greek word in 7:4 means the top of the heap, the choice part skimmed off a pile of spoil. Under the law the tithe was a wage, not charity: the Levites received a tenth of Israel's produce because they were given no land, and they paid a tenth of that on to the priests (Numbers 18:21-28). Abraham gave his tenth long before any of that existed; Paul counts 430 years from the promise to Abraham to the giving of the law (Galatians 3:17).

Priesthood ran by documented descent from Aaron, and the records mattered. When the exiles came back from Babylon, three priestly families could not find their genealogical entry and were barred from serving as unclean until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim (Ezra 2:61-63, Nehemiah 7:63-65). That is the force of 7:3 and 7:6: Melchizedek held the office with no father, mother, or line on record at all.

stories.keyTakeaway: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blessed Abraham and received a tenth from him, demonstrating his greatness; the writer argues this establishes a superior priestly order to the Levitical priesthood, one fulfilled by Jesus as an eternal priest appointed by God's oath.

stories.title: 📜 Hebrews 8
summaryBullets: The point of what we are saying is this: We do have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, (8:1).
and who ministers in the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man. (8:2).
And since every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices, it was necessary for this One also to have something to offer. (8:3).
Now if He were on earth, He would not be a priest, since there are already priests who offer gifts according to the law. (8:4).

The place where they serve is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. This is why Moses was warned when he was about to build the tabernacle: “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.” (8:5).
Now, however, Jesus has received a much more excellent ministry, just as the covenant He mediates is better and is founded on better promises. (8:6).
For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second. (8:7).
But God found fault with the people and said: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. (8:8).

It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not abide by My covenant, and I disregarded them, declares the Lord. (8:9).

For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people. (8:10).
No longer will each one teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest. (8:11).
For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.” (8:12).
By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete; and what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear. (8:13).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 31:31-34: The LORD promises a new covenant, His law written on the heart, and their sins remembered no more.
Exodus 25:9, 40: Moses is told to make the tabernacle and everything in it exactly after the pattern shown him on the mountain.
Exodus 24:12-18: Moses goes up the mountain into the cloud and stays there forty days and forty nights.
Isaiah 66:1: Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool; what house will you build for Me?
Ezekiel 36:26-27: God promises a new heart and a new spirit, and to put His own Spirit within His people.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית (berît), Greek: διαθήκη (diathḗkē, NT), Aramaic: קְיָמָא (qeyāmā)
translationNotes.note: Denotes a binding agreement; in biblical usage, God’s solemn arrangement with his people.

To serve or minister, especially in priestly duty. In Luke 1:74-75 it means serving God in holiness. In Romans 12:1 Paul applies it to presenting your life as a living sacrifice. Also used in Philippians 3:3, Hebrews 9:14, and Revelation 22:3 to show worship as lifelong service and allegiance.

translationNotes.term: The pattern shown on the mountain
translationNotes.note: Exodus 25:9 and 25:40, quoted at 8:5, tell Moses to make the tent and its furniture after the pattern he was shown. The Hebrew word means a model or a scale plan, the same word used in 1 Chronicles 28:11-19 for the written plans David handed Solomon for the temple. Nothing in the tabernacle was left to the builder's judgment.

Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full, the longest quotation in the letter. Jeremiah spoke it in Jerusalem in the last years before Nebuchadnezzar's army took the city in 586 BC and burned the temple. The promise of a covenant written on hearts rather than carried in a building was given to people who were about to lose the building, the priesthood, and the land.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jesus is a high priest seated at heaven's right hand who serves in the true sanctuary; his ministry and the new covenant he mediates are superior to the old covenant because God will write his laws on people's hearts and forgive their sins completely.

stories.title: 📜 Hebrews 9
summaryBullets: Now the first covenant had regulations for worship and also an earthly sanctuary. (9:1).
A tabernacle was prepared. In its first room were the lampstand, the table, and the consecrated bread. This was called the Holy Place. (9:2).
Behind the second curtain was a room called the Most Holy Place, (9:3).

containing the golden altar of incense and the gold-covered ark of the covenant. Inside the ark were the gold jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant. (9:4).
Above the ark were the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat. But we cannot discuss these things in detail now. (9:5).
When everything had been prepared in this way, the priests entered regularly into the first room to perform their sacred duties. (9:6).
But only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance. (9:7).
By this arrangement the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing. (9:8).
It is an illustration for the present time, because the gifts and sacrifices being offered were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper. (9:9).
They consist only in food and drink and special washings — external regulations imposed until the time of reform. (9:10).
But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, He went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. (9:11).
He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption. (9:12).
For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean sanctify them so that their bodies are clean, (9:13).
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God! (9:14).

Therefore Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, now that He has died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant. (9:15).
In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it, (9:16).
because a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died; it cannot be executed while he is still alive. (9:17).
That is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood. (9:18).

For when Moses had proclaimed every commandment of the law to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, along with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people, (9:19).
saying, “This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep.” (9:20).
In the same way, he sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and all the vessels used in worship. (9:21).
According to the law, in fact, nearly everything must be purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. (9:22).
So it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. (9:23).
For Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God. (9:24).
Nor did He enter heaven to offer Himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. (9:25).

Otherwise, Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But now He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself. (9:26).
Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment, (9:27).
so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him. (9:28).
crossRefs: Exodus 25:10-22: The ark, the gold mercy seat, and two cherubim of hammered gold, where God promises to meet and speak with Moses.
Exodus 26:31-33: The veil of blue, purple, and scarlet with cherubim worked into it, dividing the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.
Leviticus 16:1-34: The Day of Atonement: the high priest enters behind the veil with blood, and the second goat is sent into the wilderness.
Numbers 19:1-10: A red heifer is burned outside the camp and its ashes are kept for the water of cleansing.
Exodus 24:3-8: Moses reads the Book of the Covenant, throws blood on the people, and says, This is the blood of the covenant.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית (berît), Greek: διαθήκη (diathḗkē, NT), Aramaic: קְיָמָא (qeyāmā)
translationNotes.note: Denotes a binding agreement; in biblical usage, God’s solemn arrangement with his people.

To serve or minister, especially in priestly duty. In Luke 1:74-75 it means serving God in holiness. In Romans 12:1 Paul applies it to presenting your life as a living sacrifice. Also used in Philippians 3:3, Hebrews 9:14, and Revelation 22:3 to show worship as lifelong service and allegiance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַחַת לְעוֹלָם (ʾaḥat ləʿōlām, sense), Greek: ἐφάπαξ (ephápax, NT), Aramaic: חדא לעלמין (ḥadā l-ʿālmīn)
translationNotes.note: Phrase stresses Christ’s sacrifice as unique, sufficient, and not to be repeated.

A small, fragrant herb (Origanum syriacum / Syrian oregano), growing in rocky soil. Bunches of hyssop were used to apply Passover blood to the doorposts (Exodus 12:22), in leper-cleansing rituals (Leviticus 14:6), and held up to Jesus on the cross with a wine-soaked sponge (John 19:29).

translationNotes.term: The lampstand, the table, and the bread of the Presence
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְנוֹרָה (menorah) - Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים (lechem happanim)
translationNotes.note: The outer room held two pieces of furniture. The lampstand was hammered from a single talent of pure gold, about 75 pounds, with six branches off a central shaft, and Aaron trimmed its seven lamps with beaten olive oil every morning and evening (Exodus 25:31-40, 27:20-21). The table carried twelve loaves in two rows of six with frankincense beside them, replaced every sabbath, and the old loaves were eaten by the priests inside the holy place (Leviticus 24:5-9). That is the bread David asked for at Nob when his men were hungry (1 Samuel 21:1-6).

Two curtains hung in the tabernacle, one at the entrance and one inside. The inner one was woven of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn with fine linen and had cherubim worked into it, hanging on four gold-covered posts (Exodus 26:31-33). It was a door nobody opened: the high priest passed it one day a year, and no one else ever. At the crucifixion it tore from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִזְבַּח הַקְּטֹרֶת (mizbach haqqetoret) - Greek: θυμιατήριον (thymiaterion)
translationNotes.note: A small altar of acacia overlaid with gold, one cubit square and two cubits high, roughly 18 inches by 18 inches and three feet tall, with a horn at each corner (Exodus 30:1-10). Incense burned on it every morning and evening, made to a fixed recipe of stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense that no one was allowed to copy for private use (Exodus 30:34-38). Its one blood rite each year belonged to the Day of Atonement, when the high priest also carried a censer of its coals through the veil so the smoke would cover the mercy seat (Exodus 30:10, Leviticus 16:12-13); 1 Kings 6:22 speaks of the altar as belonging to the inner sanctuary.

translationNotes.term: The ark of the covenant and what was in it
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרוֹן הַבְּרִית (aron habberit) - Hebrew: מָן (man)
translationNotes.note: A chest of acacia wood overlaid inside and out with gold, two and a half cubits by one and a half by one and a half, roughly 45 by 27 by 27 inches, carried on gold-covered poles that were never taken out of its rings (Exodus 25:10-16). Hebrews 9:4 lists what it held: the stone tablets Moses brought down the second time (Deuteronomy 10:1-5); a gold jar of the manna, the bread that appeared each morning and took its name from the people's own question, man hu, what is it (Exodus 16:14-15, 31-34); and Aaron's staff, one of twelve laid up overnight in the tent, which alone budded, blossomed, and grew ripe almonds by morning (Numbers 17:1-11).

translationNotes.term: The mercy seat and the cherubim
translationNotes.note: The lid of the ark was solid gold with two cherubim hammered out of the same piece, one at each end, facing each other with their wings spread over it (Exodus 25:17-22). It was not ornament and not a chair; it was the spot God named for meeting Moses, and Numbers 7:89 says the voice came from above it, between the two cherubim. The Greek Old Testament calls it the hilasterion, the place of atonement, and that is the word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים (Yom haKippurim) - Hebrew: עֲזָאזֵל (azazel)
translationNotes.note: The single day behind 9:7 and 9:25 is set out in Leviticus 16. On the tenth day of the seventh month the high priest bathed and put on plain linen instead of his gold vestments, killed a bull for his own sins, then cast lots over two goats, one marked for the LORD and one for Azazel. He carried blood through the veil and sprinkled it on the front of the mercy seat and seven times before it, the bull's first and then the goat's; over the living goat he confessed the sins of Israel and a man led it out into the wilderness. The bodies of the bull and goat were burned outside the camp, and the whole nation fasted and did no work that day (Leviticus 16:27-31, 23:26-32).

translationNotes.term: The ashes of a red heifer
translationNotes.note: Numbers 19 called for a red cow without defect that had never worn a yoke. It was taken outside the camp and killed in front of the priest, who sprinkled its blood seven times toward the tent, and then the whole animal was burned, hide, flesh, blood, and dung, with cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool thrown into the fire. The ashes were stored and stirred into fresh water, and that water was sprinkled on the third day and the seventh on anyone who had touched a corpse, a bone, or a grave. Everyone who handled the rite, the priest included, was himself unclean until evening.

translationNotes.term: A will and a covenant in one word
translationNotes.note: One Greek word, diatheke, stands behind both covenant and will in this chapter. In everyday first-century Greek it was the word for a last will and testament, an arrangement one man lays down and nobody negotiates with him about; the Greek Old Testament also used it to render the Hebrew word for covenant, berit. Hebrews 9:15-18 works both senses at once, which is why English versions read covenant in 9:15, will in 9:16-17, and covenant again in 9:18.

stories.keyTakeaway: The tabernacle's layout and priesthood regulations are detailed, with only the high priest entering the inner sanctuary once yearly; Christ replaces this system by entering heaven itself once with his own blood, obtaining eternal redemption and a new covenant.

stories.title: 📜 Hebrews 10
summaryBullets: For the law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves. It can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship. (10:1).
If it could, would not the offerings have ceased? For the worshipers would have been cleansed once for all, and would no longer have felt the guilt of their sins. (10:2).
Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, (10:3).
because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. (10:4).
Therefore, when Christ came into the world, He said: “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me. (10:5).
In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight. (10:6).
Then I said, ‘Here I am, it is written about Me in the scroll: I have come to do Your will, O God.’” (10:7).
In the passage above He says, “Sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not desire, nor did You delight in them” (although they are offered according to the law). (10:8).
Then He adds, “Here I am, I have come to do Your will.” He takes away the first to establish the second. (10:9).
And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. (10:10).
Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. (10:11).
But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God. (10:12).
Since that time, He waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet, (10:13).
because by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified. (10:14).
The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. First He says: (10:15).
“This is the covenant I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.” (10:16).
Then He adds: “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” (10:17).
And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed. (10:18).
Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, (10:19).
by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body, (10:20).
and since we have a great priest over the house of God, (10:21).
let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water. (10:22).
Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful. (10:23).
And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. (10:24).
Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching. (10:25).
If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains, (10:26).
but only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries. (10:27).
Anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. (10:28).
How much more severely do you think one deserves to be punished who has trampled on the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him, and insulted the Spirit of grace? (10:29).
For we know Him who said, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge His people.” (10:30).
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. (10:31).
Remember the early days that you were in the light. In those days, you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering. (10:32).
Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution; at other times you were partners with those who were so treated. (10:33).
You sympathized with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession. (10:34).
So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward. (10:35).
You need to persevere, so that after you have done the will of God, you will receive what He has promised. (10:36).
For, “In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay. (10:37).
But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.” (10:38).
But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls. (10:39).
crossRefs: Psalm 40:6-8: Sacrifice and offering You did not desire; then I said, Here I am, I have come to do Your will.
Isaiah 1:11-15: The LORD says He takes no pleasure in the blood of bulls and lambs and goats offered by hands full of blood.
Deuteronomy 17:6: A man is put to death on the testimony of two or three witnesses, never on the word of one.
Deuteronomy 32:35-36: Vengeance is Mine, I will repay; the LORD will judge His people.
Habakkuk 2:3-4: The vision waits for its appointed time; the righteous will live by his faith.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית (berît), Greek: διαθήκη (diathḗkē, NT), Aramaic: קְיָמָא (qeyāmā)
translationNotes.note: Denotes a binding agreement; in biblical usage, God’s solemn arrangement with his people.

To serve or minister, especially in priestly duty. In Luke 1:74-75 it means serving God in holiness. In Romans 12:1 Paul applies it to presenting your life as a living sacrifice. Also used in Philippians 3:3, Hebrews 9:14, and Revelation 22:3 to show worship as lifelong service and allegiance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַחַת לְעוֹלָם (ʾaḥat ləʿōlām, sense), Greek: ἐφάπαξ (ephápax, NT), Aramaic: חדא לעלמין (ḥadā l-ʿālmīn)
translationNotes.note: Phrase stresses Christ’s sacrifice as unique, sufficient, and not to be repeated.

Hebrew does not make a covenant; it cuts one, and the phrase is literal. In Genesis 15:9-18 the animals are cut in half and the halves laid opposite each other, and a smoking firepot and a flaming torch pass between the pieces; Jeremiah 34:18-19 names the officials who walked between the parts of a calf and then broke their word. At Sinai Moses threw half the blood against the altar and half over the people and said, This is the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:6-8). Those are the words 10:29 uses of trampling that blood.

The verb in 10:33 means to be put on a stage; it is built on the word for theatre. Paul uses the noun the same way when he says the apostles have been made a spectacle to the world (1 Corinthians 4:9). The next verse names what came with it, seized property and prison, and a Roman prison did not feed its prisoners, so the two went together.

Hebrews 10:11-12 sets a standing priest against a seated one, and the point is furniture. The tabernacle inventory in Exodus 25-27 lists an ark, a table, a lampstand, an altar, and a basin, and no chair for a priest. Priests worked on their feet, and the work never stopped: Exodus 29:38-42 fixes two lambs every day, one at morning and one at twilight, with no end date.

stories.keyTakeaway: Christ's single sacrifice has made believers perfect forever, unlike the repeated animal sacrifices of the law; the author exhorts readers to hold fast to faith, meet together, and remember their past endurance, warning that deliberate rejection of this truth brings severe judgment.

stories.title: 🌿 Hebrews 11
summaryBullets: Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. (11:1).
This is why the ancients were commended. (11:2).
By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible. (11:3).
By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. By faith he was commended as righteous when God gave approval to his gifts. And by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead. (11:4).
By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death: “He could not be found, because God had taken him away.” For before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God. (11:5).
And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him. (11:6).
By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family. By faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith. (11:7).
By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going. (11:8).
By faith he dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise. (11:9).
For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God. (11:10).
By faith Sarah, even though she was barren and beyond the proper age, was enabled to conceive a child, because she considered Him faithful who had promised. (11:11).
And so from one man, and he as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore. (11:12).

All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar. And they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. (11:13).
Now those who say such things show that they are seeking a country of their own. (11:14).
If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had opportunity to return. (11:15).
Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them. (11:16).
By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar. He who had received the promises was ready to offer his one and only son, (11:17).
even though God had said to him, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” (11:18).
Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death. (11:19).
By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future. (11:20).
By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. (11:21).
By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones. (11:22).
By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king’s edict. (11:23).
By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. (11:24).
He chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin. (11:25).
He valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to his reward. (11:26).
By faith Moses left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; he persevered because he saw Him who is invisible. (11:27).
By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s own firstborn. (11:28).
By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land; but when the Egyptians tried to follow, they were drowned. (11:29).
By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days. (11:30).
By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient. (11:31).
And what more shall I say? Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, (11:32).
who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised; who shut the mouths of lions, (11:33).
quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword; who gained strength from weakness, became mighty in battle, and put foreign armies to flight. (11:34).
Women received back their dead, raised to life again. Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection. (11:35).
Still others endured mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. (11:36).
They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated. (11:37).
The world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground. (11:38).
These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised. (11:39).
God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect. (11:40).
crossRefs: Genesis 4:3-8: Abel brings the firstborn of his flock and the LORD looks with favour on his offering; Cain kills him.
Genesis 5:21-24: Enoch walked with God for three hundred years, and he was not, because God took him away.
Genesis 22:1-14: Abraham is told to offer Isaac, and a ram caught in a thicket is provided in his place.
Exodus 12:21-23: Israel puts the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorframes and the destroyer passes over the house.
Joshua 2:1-21: Rahab hides the spies in Jericho, lets them down through her window, and ties a scarlet cord in it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱמוּנָה (ʾĕmûnāh), Greek: πίστις (pístis, NT), Aramaic: הֵימָנוּתָא (hēymānūṯā)
translationNotes.note: Carries sense of trust, confidence, or faithfulness; Hebrews 11 defines it as assurance of hope and conviction of unseen realities.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְכוּת בִּלְתִּי מוֹט (malkût biltî mōṭ, sense), Greek: βασιλείαν ἀσάλευτον (basileían asáleyton, NT), Aramaic: מלכותא דלא מתזיע (malkūtā d-lā mtazīaʿ)
translationNotes.note: Describes the eternal reign of God, contrasted with things of creation that can be shaken and removed.

The word in 11:35 names a particular execution: the victim was stretched over a frame or wheel, drum-tight, and beaten to death. The account behind it is 2 Maccabees 6-7, from the persecution under Antiochus IV in the 160s BC, where an old scribe named Eleazar and then a mother with seven sons were tortured to death after refusing release in exchange for eating swine's flesh, saying they looked to be raised again.

Jewish tradition attached this line to Isaiah. The Martyrdom of Isaiah, a Second Temple Jewish work, says King Manasseh had him sawn in half with a wooden saw, and the Babylonian Talmud records the same execution at Yevamot 49b. Manasseh's reign is the one 2 Kings 21:16 describes as filling Jerusalem with innocent blood from end to end.

Rahab kept a house built into the wall of Jericho, which is how she could let the spies down on a rope through her window after the city gate was shut behind the search party (Joshua 2:15). The scarlet cord she left hanging there marked the house to be spared, and Joshua 6:22-25 says she and her whole family were brought out alive and settled among Israel. Matthew 1:5 lists her in the line of David.

stories.keyTakeaway: The author defines faith as confidence in unseen things and catalogs the faithful acts of Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, and others who obeyed God without receiving the promises in their lifetimes. He notes that some faithful were tortured and killed while wandering destitute, yet all were commended for their faith.

stories.title: 🌿 Hebrews 12
summaryBullets: Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us. (12:1).
Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. (12:2).
Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart. (12:3).
In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood. (12:4).
And you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: “My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. (12:5).
For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives.” (12:6).
Endure suffering as discipline; God is treating you as sons. For what son is not disciplined by his father? (12:7).
If you do not experience discipline like everyone else, then you are illegitimate children and not true sons. (12:8).
Furthermore, we have all had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live? (12:9).
Our fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness. (12:10).
No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it. (12:11).
Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees. (12:12).
Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed. (12:13).
Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord. (12:14).
See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many. (12:15).
See to it that no one is sexually immoral, or is godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright. (12:16).
For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears. (12:17).
For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm; (12:18).
to a trumpet blast or to a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken. (12:19).
For they could not bear what was commanded: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.” (12:20).
The sight was so terrifying that even Moses said, “I am trembling with fear.” (12:21).
Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels (12:22).
in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, (12:23).
to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. (12:24).

See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks. For if the people did not escape when they refused Him who warned them on earth, how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven? (12:25).
At that time His voice shook the earth, but now He has promised, “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.” (12:26).
The words “Once more” signify the removal of what can be shaken — that is, created things — so that the unshakable may remain. (12:27).
Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. (12:28).
“For our God is a consuming fire.” (12:29).
crossRefs: Proverbs 3:11-12: My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline, for the LORD corrects the one He loves, as a father the son he delights in.
Genesis 25:29-34: Esau comes in famished and sells his birthright to Jacob for bread and lentil stew, and despises it.
Deuteronomy 21:15-17: The firstborn must receive a double share of the inheritance and cannot be passed over for a favoured wife's son.
Exodus 19:12-19: A boundary is set around Sinai on pain of death; the mountain burns and smokes and the trumpet grows louder and louder.
Haggai 2:6-7: Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land.
