translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְכוּת בִּלְתִּי מוֹט (malkût biltî mōṭ, sense), Greek: βασιλείαν ἀσάλευτον (basileían asáleyton, NT), Aramaic: מלכותא דלא מתזיע (malkūtā d-lā mtazīaʿ)
translationNotes.note: Describes the eternal reign of God, contrasted with things of creation that can be shaken and removed.

translationNotes.term: The cloud of witnesses and the race
translationNotes.original: Greek: μάρτυς (martys) - Greek: ὄγκος (onkos) - Greek: ἀγών (agon)
translationNotes.note: The scene in 12:1 is a stadium. The agon is a contest, the word used for the Greek games; the onkos thrown off is bulk or dead weight, what a runner strips before the start. The martys is a witness in the courtroom sense, one who gives testimony, which is what the long list of names in chapter 11 has just done; the same Greek word gives English the word martyr.

A birthright was property and authority, not sentiment: a double share of the estate, which the law protected even against a father's preference for a favoured wife's son (Deuteronomy 21:15-17), plus headship of the family after his death. Esau traded his for bread and lentil stew when he came in from the field starving, and Genesis 25:34 says outright that he despised it. The red stew is why he is also called Edom, which means red; when he later wanted the blessing, it was already gone (Genesis 27:34-38).

translationNotes.term: The mountain that can be touched
translationNotes.note: Hebrews 12:18-21 is describing Sinai in Exodus 19-20. A boundary was set around the mountain and anyone who touched it, man or animal, was to be stoned or shot with arrows rather than approached (Exodus 19:12-13). There was thunder, a thick cloud, fire, smoke, an earthquake, and a trumpet blast growing louder, and the people stood at a distance and begged that God stop speaking to them directly (Exodus 20:18-19). The words of Moses quoted in 12:21 come from Deuteronomy 9:19.

stories.keyTakeaway: The author exhorts readers to run the race of faith by fixing their eyes on Jesus, who endured the cross; he frames God's discipline as evidence of legitimate sonship and calls believers to pursue holiness and peace, contrasting the terrifying old covenant with access to the heavenly Jerusalem through Christ's new covenant.

stories.title: 🕊️ Hebrews 13
summaryBullets: Continue in brotherly love. (13:1).
Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it. (13:2).
Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them. (13:3).
Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers. (13:4).
Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.” (13:5).
So we say with confidence: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?” (13:6).
Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith. (13:7).
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. (13:8).
Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them. (13:9).
We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat. (13:10).
Although the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin, the bodies are burned outside the camp. (13:11).
And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood. (13:12).
Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore. (13:13).
For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come. (13:14).
Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. (13:15).
And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased. (13:16).

Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you. (13:17).
Pray for us; we are convinced that we have a clear conscience and desire to live honorably in every way. (13:18).
And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon. (13:19).
Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, (13:20).
equip you with every good thing to do His will. And may He accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. (13:21).
I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly. (13:22).
Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you. (13:23).
Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send you greetings. (13:24).
Grace be with all of you. (13:25).
crossRefs: Genesis 18:2-3: Abraham entertains angels unawares.
Malachi 3:6: The Lord does not change.
Psalm 118:6: The Lord is my helper; I will not fear.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶבַח תּוֹדָה (zeḇaḥ tôdāh), Greek: θυσία αἰνέσεως (thysía aineseōs, NT), Aramaic: דבח תודתא (dabḥa ṭōdātā)
translationNotes.note: Phrase for an offering of thanksgiving; in Hebrews used figuratively for continual verbal praise to God.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה (michutz lammachaneh) - Greek: ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς (exo tes paremboles)
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 16:27 disposed of the Day of Atonement offerings the same way every year: the animals whose blood had gone into the sanctuary were carried right out of the camp, and hide, flesh, and dung were burned on the ash heap, with the man who did it washing his clothes afterwards (Leviticus 4:11-12). Outside the camp was also where a condemned man was taken to die (Leviticus 24:14, Numbers 15:35-36). Hebrews 13:12 puts the crucifixion in that place: Jesus suffered outside the city gate (John 19:17-20).

The Greek word for hospitality means love of strangers. Hebrews 13:2 is pointing at specific cases: Abraham ran to meet three travellers at Mamre and had a calf killed for them (Genesis 18:1-8), Lot took two visitors in off the square at Sodom (Genesis 19:1-3), Gideon fed a visitor under the oak at Ophrah (Judges 6:11-24), and Manoah and his wife did the same (Judges 13:15-21). None of them knew who they were feeding until afterwards.

A Roman prison did not feed you. Food, clothing, and money came from outside or not at all, which is why access mattered: Felix gave orders that Paul's friends be allowed to attend to his needs (Acts 24:23), Epaphroditus carried a gift from Philippi to Paul in custody (Philippians 4:18), and Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found him (2 Timothy 1:16-17). Paul in Rome was chained to a soldier (Acts 28:16, 20), so visiting a prisoner was a public act with a price attached.

stories.keyTakeaway: The letter closes with practical exhortations for love, purity, contentment, perseverance, obedience to leaders, and a benediction of peace and grace.

intro:
Hebrews does not name its author. The text is anonymous, opening not with the standard Pauline greeting but with a majestic theological prologue ("Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son," Hebrews 1:1-2). The recipients are Jewish Christians, likely living in Italy (Hebrews 13:24, "Those who come from Italy send you greetings," is most naturally read as the writer greeting Italian readers on behalf of Italian believers presently with him outside Italy), facing pressure to abandon their confession of Christ and return to the visible familiar worship of the Second Temple system. The date of composition is pre-AD 70: throughout the letter the Levitical priesthood and temple sacrifices are described in the present tense as ongoing activities (Hebrews 5:1-4; 7:27-28; 8:3-5; 9:6-9; 9:25; 10:1-3, 8, 11: "Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins"), an argument that would have been pointless if the temple had already been destroyed by Titus in AD 70 (the temple's destruction by Roman armies under Titus would have been the strongest possible illustration of the letter's argument and would surely have been mentioned). Composition therefore most likely falls between AD 60 and AD 68, before the Jewish-Roman War (AD 66-73) brought the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, and during the period of growing imperial persecution under Nero (AD 64 onward).

Scripture does not name the author, and the early church never reached a single settled consensus. Several candidates have been proposed within Bible-affirming tradition, all of them members of Paul's apostolic circle or near-contemporaries. (1) Paul: the dominant view in the Eastern church from the second century onward, formally accepted at the Council of Hippo (AD 393) and the Councils of Carthage (AD 397, 419). If Paul is the author, the absence of his customary signature is best explained by the strained relationship between Paul and the Jerusalem Jewish-Christian community, who associated his name with the Gentile mission and might have rejected a letter openly bearing his name; the writing style differs from Paul's other letters, but this could reflect amanuensis-mediated composition (Origen noted that the "thoughts" might be Paul's while the "phrasing" was someone else's). (2) Barnabas: proposed by Tertullian (c. AD 200, in On Modesty 20) and held by part of the North African church; Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36) whose familiarity with the priestly system would fit the letter's themes. (3) Apollos: proposed by Martin Luther in the 16th century and held by many since; Apollos was a "Jew, a native of Alexandria, an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures" (Acts 18:24), whose Alexandrian rhetorical training and scriptural fluency match the letter's polished Greek and dense Old Testament argumentation. (4) Clement of Rome: proposed by Origen (c. AD 230) as one possibility (Origen famously concluded "but who actually wrote the epistle, God only knows"); Clement was the late-first-century bishop of Rome whose own Letter to the Corinthians (1 Clement, c. AD 96) heavily quotes Hebrews. (5) Luke: also suggested by Origen as a possibility; the polished Greek style would fit Luke's training, but the differences from Luke-Acts make this candidate less probable. (6) Priscilla (with or without Aquila): proposed by Adolf von Harnack and others since the 19th century; Priscilla was the wife of Aquila (Acts 18:2, 18, 26; Romans 16:3; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19) and an accomplished teacher who had instructed Apollos in the way of God (Acts 18:26), and her anonymity would be naturally explained by the cultural reluctance to receive a letter openly authored by a woman. Origen's third-century summary remains the honest conclusion: "Who wrote the epistle, in truth God knows."

The historical setting is the Roman Empire in the late 60s AD, with the Jewish-Roman War approaching or just beginning, the Neronian persecution of Christians having begun in AD 64, and the Jerusalem temple system still operating as it had for centuries. The recipients of the letter were apparently a Jewish-Christian community (or perhaps a house church within a larger community) experiencing significant pressure: they had endured an earlier persecution that had cost them property (Hebrews 10:32-34, "But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings... you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property"); some of their members had been imprisoned (Hebrews 13:3); they were tempted to drift back to the safer, visible, socially acceptable observance of Jewish temple worship rather than continue to be identified with the despised name of Jesus. The writer addresses this temptation by arguing that Christ is supremely greater than every Old Testament category to which the readers might retreat: greater than the angels (Hebrews 1:5-2:18), greater than Moses (3:1-6), greater than Aaron and the Levitical high priests (4:14-5:10; 7:1-28), greater than the old covenant (8:1-13), greater than the earthly sanctuary (9:1-28), greater than the repeated animal sacrifices (10:1-18). The letter is the New Testament's most extended explanation of the relationship between the Old Testament priestly and sacrificial system and Christ's once-for-all atoning work. Christ's full deity is repeatedly affirmed: Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature"; Hebrews 1:8 quotes Psalm 45:6-7 and applies it directly to the Son: "Of the Son he says, 'Your throne, O God, is forever and ever'"; Hebrews 13:8 declares, "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever."

Hebrews is the fifty-eighth book of the Christian Bible and the nineteenth book of the New Testament. The letter has thirteen chapters. In the Eastern canonical traditions Hebrews was placed among Paul's letters (since the East accepted Pauline authorship), often between 2 Thessalonians and 1 Timothy; in the Western canonical tradition Hebrews was placed after Philemon, separate from the Pauline corpus (since the West was more skeptical of Pauline authorship), the order preserved in modern English Bibles. The earliest surviving manuscript of Hebrews is Papyrus 46 (P46, the Chester Beatty II papyrus, c. AD 175-225), which places Hebrews immediately after Romans within the Pauline corpus (reflecting the Eastern position that Hebrews is Paul's); other early witnesses include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). Several of Hebrews' passages have become foundational to Christian theology and worship: Hebrews 1:1-4 (the prologue's declaration of Christ's full deity and creative work); Hebrews 4:12 ("the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword"); Hebrews 4:14-16 (the great high priest's invitation to "draw near to the throne of grace with confidence"); Hebrews 9:27 ("it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment"); Hebrews 11 (the great "hall of faith" listing Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and the "cloud of witnesses"); Hebrews 12:1-2 ("let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith"); and Hebrews 13:8 ("Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever").
